paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder. Seizures begin in the neonatal period or early infancy and are followed by severe to profound developmental delay and intellectual disability. Chatron et al. (2020) described it as a syndromic disorder in which the encephalopathy is variably associated with cleft palate, joint contractures and/or pes equinovarus, and omphalocele. Neuray et al. (2020) emphasized early-infantile onset epilepsy and hypotonia, with variable non-CNS features such as skeletal abnormalities, dysmorphic features, and cleft palate.

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) reported 11 patients from 6 unrelated consanguineous families of Algerian, Egyptian, Turkish (2 families), Iranian, and Brazilian origin. In all 10 patients whose early history was available, seizures began in the first month of life. Seizures at onset were mainly myoclonic seizures (5 patients) or epileptic spasms (6 patients). Seven of the 8 patients with neonatal recordings had a suppression-burst or burst-attenuation EEG pattern at onset, and the 2 patients first recorded later had hypsarrhythmia. Six patients eventually achieved seizure control with antiepileptic drugs. All living patients had severe psychomotor delay, and intellectual disability was profound in every patient who could be assessed. Brain MRI was normal in 5 patients. Head circumference was normal in all but 1 patient. Seven patients had cleft palate, 6 had joint contractures, 5 had pes equinovarus, and 4 had scoliosis. Both patients from one family had omphalocele. Three patients had facial dysmorphic features without clear common elements. Four patients died before 4 years of age. The authors described markedly increased muscle tone as a core clinical feature, although patients often had axial hypotonia.

paragraphs.text: In family A of Chatron et al. (2020), 2 sibs were born to first-cousin parents of Algerian origin, and both had cleft soft palate. The boy was first seen at 5 months of age with developmental regression, loss of visual contact, opisthotonus, axial hypotonia, and hypsarrhythmia on EEG. Brain MRI and metabolic screening of blood, urine, and CSF were normal. At 6 years of age he could not sit unassisted, had spastic tetraparesis, and had no verbal communication. His sister was admitted at 2 days of age with eye revulsion, cyanosis, and spasm-like movements, and her EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern. Her seizures were controlled at 3 months with levetiracetam and vigabatrin. At 26 months she had severe developmental delay, axial hypotonia, no head control, segmental hypertonia, no visual contact, and no verbal communication.

paragraphs.text: In family B of Chatron et al. (2020), 2 sibs were born to first-cousin Egyptian parents. In the girl, prenatal scanning detected a liver-containing omphalocele, intestinal atresia, and right talipes equinovarus. She also had cleft soft palate, multiple dysmorphic features (including hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, microretrognathia, and abnormal low-set ears), and limited movement of all joints with camptodactyly. Further findings were scoliosis, skin hemangiomas, and genital anomalies (a large clitoris with hypoplastic labia). Seizures, consisting of eye twitches and epileptic spasms, began at 2 weeks of age. Her EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern that evolved to hypsarrhythmia, and she became seizure-free on vigabatrin at 9 months. Brain MRI showed a hypoplastic corpus callosum and progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy. She died at 2 years of age of failure to thrive and respiratory infection. Her brother had omphalocele, bilateral talipes equinovarus, arthrogryposis, failure to thrive, and seizures from 2 weeks of age, with dysmorphism similar to his sister's. He became seizure-free on vigabatrin at 2 years and died at 4 years of age.

paragraphs.text: In family C of Chatron et al. (2020), 2 sibs were born to a first-cousin Turkish couple. The 12-year-old girl had eyelid myoclonia from 2 weeks of age and generalized tonic-clonic seizures from 5 months. Her initial EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern, and her epilepsy was refractory. She had profound intellectual disability, tetraparesis with increased muscle tone, cleft palate, talipes, and conductive hearing loss. Brain MRI was normal. Her brother had refractory myoclonic, tonic, and tonic-clonic seizures from the first day of life, cleft palate, and a suppression-burst EEG, and he died from refractory seizures at 2 years of age. Both grandfathers had adult-onset tonic-clonic seizures. The authors did not assume that these seizures were caused by the same genetic defect.

His features included facial dysmorphism, cleft palate, Hirschsprung disease, pes equinovarus, flexion contractures of the elbows and knees, cervical and axillary webbing, and hypotonia. Epileptic spasms had been present from 1 month of age, and his EEG showed hypsarrhythmia. Brain CT showed minimal hydrocephalus and an atlantoaxial anomaly. He also had nystagmus, pale optic discs, failed hearing testing at 1 year, recurrent aspiration pneumonia, and grade 1 nephrocalcinosis. paragraphs.text: Neuray et al. (2020) reported 6 patients from 6 unrelated families of Persian, Pakistani, African American, Sudanese, Egyptian, and Turkish ancestry. Most were born to consanguineous parents, and all were born at term after a normal pregnancy. Seizures began between 2 and 6 months of age and were predominantly focal motor seizures with or without impaired awareness. Two patients also had epileptic spasms, 4 had focal non-motor seizures, and 5 had bilateral motor seizures. Seizures were controlled in 3 patients and drug-resistant in 3. EEG at onset showed burst suppression in 2 patients, diffuse slowing with multifocal and generalized sharp waves in 2, and hypsarrhythmia in 2. Brain MRI was normal except in 2 patients, one with slight ventricular enlargement and one with moderate global atrophy. All patients had severe developmental delay, and intellectual development did not accelerate even after seizure control. Most never achieved speech or non-verbal communication; only 1 developed simple speech. Five patients had reduced muscle strength, and 4 had limited head control or could not sit or crawl. Two patients depended on a nasogastric tube because of dysphagia. Four had mild dysmorphic facial features, and only 1 had cleft palate. Other features without clear common elements were hirsutism, kidney stones, urogenital malformations, diastasis recti, reduced head circumference, clinodactyly, short arms, arthrogryposis of the lower limbs, and congenital hip dislocation. Metabolic workups were normal.

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) studied 11 patients with DEE89 from 6 consanguineous families using whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing. In all affected individuals, they identified rare homozygous variants in the GAD1 gene, which were retained as the only likely pathogenic variants. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the variants segregated with the disease in all families. Four of the 6 families carried variants predicted to truncate the protein: a splice site mutation, a frameshift, and a nonsense mutation (R531X) that was shared by an Iranian and a Turkish family. One family carried an in-frame deletion of a conserved lysine (K232del), and one carried a missense mutation (E509K). In family A, cDNA analysis of parental lymphoblastoid cells showed that the splice site mutation produced no normal mRNA. In family B, the K232del protein was expressed at a level comparable to wildtype in a cell-free expression system.
